paper_metadata.title: A 62mW Stereo Class-G Headphone Driver with 108dB Dynamic Range and 600μA/Channel Quiescent Current Jianlong Chen1, Sasi Kumar Arunachalam1, Todd L. Brooks1, Iuri Mehr1, Felix Cheung1, Hariprasath Venkatram2

figures.caption: Figure 10.6.3 shows the overall headphone driver architecture. Headphone drivers usually need a high-order loop filter to suppress non-linearity and power supply disturbance from the output stage [1][2]. Taking advantage of the high gain associated with the adaptive class-B control scheme, a simple first-order loop filter is sufficient to suppress non-linearity and battery power supply variation. Part of the variation is due to the class-G operation. When the output voltage rises above a threshold, the supply for the driver output stage is increased. If the output voltage is below the threshold, the supply is reduced in an efficient way, using a charge pump (class-G supply as shown in Fig. 10.6.3). A first-order Gm-C filter is used as loop filter. The transconductance cell is implemented as a low-noise, high voltage gain input stage followed by a 1/R second stage to reduce the overall Gm value. Hence, the overall Gm is defined by the input differential pair (transistors M1/M2) gm divided by R2/R1 ratio. This transconductance topology allows using a smaller value capacitor C while achieving low input-referred noise. With an R2/R1 ratio of 25, only a 4pF loading capacitor C

references.sentence: A more efficient approach is to use a hybrid topology where a class AB amplifier is used for small signals, and an additional class B amplifier provides the large signal [1], as shown in Fig. 10.6.1.
An adaptive class-B driver control scheme is developed to overcome threshold mismatch, as shown in Fig 10.6.2.
Fig. 10.6.2 also shows the smooth transition between class-AB and class-B output currents for the full scale excursion of the output signal.
Figure 10.6.3 shows the overall headphone driver architecture.
If the output voltage is below the threshold, the supply is reduced in an efficient way, using a charge pump (class-G supply as shown in Fig. 10.6.3).
A digital sequence-based PCN suppression scheme using an auxiliary output stage is shown in Fig. 10.6.4.
Figure 10.6.5 shows the plot of measured THD+N versus output power for a 1 kHz sinusoid input signal with a 32Ω load and the measured PCN during powerup and power-down.
All measurement results and comparison with recent state-of-the-art work are summarized in Fig. 10.6.6.
The die micrograph given in Fig. 10.6.7 shows the stereo driver area is 0.32mm2 excluding the class-G supply circuitry.
